title: Welcome to the EquitySight Blog
excerpt: Why we're launching a long-form blog for Australian property investors, and what you can expect from us over the coming months.
body_md:
## Why a blog

EquitySight has always been a calculator first — the 9 free tools, the full 30-year projection, the suburb insight pages. Those products are numeric. They tell you *what* the numbers are.

But numbers alone don't teach strategy. A first home buyer asking whether to use Queensland's Shared Equity Scheme, a Pro subscriber deciding whether to refinance into an offset loan, an investor weighing rental yield against capital growth — they all need context, not just a calculator output.

That's the gap this blog is meant to fill.

## What we'll cover

We're writing four themes into the editorial calendar:

- **Market cycles.** The Australian market is not a single market — Sydney, Melbourne, Perth, and Brisbane move on different rhythms. We'll explain what the RBA cash rate, the APRA buffer, and the unemployment rate actually mean for suburb-level demand.
- **Tax structure.** Negative gearing, depreciation schedules, ATO capital-gains reporting, the PPR exemption — all explained from a cash-flow perspective.
- **Strategy playbooks.** Buy-and-hold, rental yield, renovation, subdivision, co-ownership. Each with its own cash-flow profile and tax treatment.
- **First home buyer schemes.** State-by-state deep dives on the Shared Equity, HomeBuilder, First Home Guarantee, and related programs.

Everything we publish will be referenced, dated, and linked back to the underlying data source. If it came from the ABS, we'll say so. If it came from the RBA, we'll say so. If it's opinion, we'll label it.

## Who's writing

Our founder **Alex Chen** and data lead **James Patel** share writing duties. Alex covers the finance and modelling side — cash flow, LMI, LVR, amortisation. James covers the data side — census indicators, suburb trends, scheme eligibility. Our head of product **Sarah Williams** edits every post for clarity and reviews the visual design.

We're explicit about our editorial standards: no sponsored content, no paid placements, no affiliate links without disclosure, and every correction logged publicly in the [methodology change log](/methodology.html#11-change-log).

## What to expect next

Our next three articles:

1. *How the RBA cash rate feeds into your actual repayment* — with worked examples
2. *The real cost of LMI vs. saving a larger deposit* — break-even analysis
3. *Victoria's First Home Owner Grant vs. the stamp-duty concession* — a scenario-by-scenario comparison

If you want a specific topic covered, email [editorial@equitysight.app](mailto:editorial@equitysight.app). We read every email.

Thanks for reading — and welcome aboard.
author: Alex Chen
author_bio: Co-founder and CTO of EquitySight. Built the original shared-equity model after buying his first home in Brisbane through the QLD Shared Equity Scheme. 10 years in Australian fintech engineering before co-founding EquitySight.

title: How We Score 3,022 Australian Suburbs — Behind the Numbers
excerpt: A walk-through of the EquitySight investment-score formula, the noindex gate, and the state-median comparison deltas that drive every suburb profile on the site.
body_md:
## The short version

Every number on an EquitySight suburb profile — investment score, strategy verdict, risk factor, outlook, comparison table — is computed deterministically from published government data. Nothing is guessed, estimated, or hand-written per suburb. This article walks through the formulas in plain English so you can see exactly how a suburb ends up with the score it does.

If you prefer the raw formulas, our [methodology page](/methodology.html) has them in one place.

## What goes into a score

The investment score is out of 100, and it's the weighted sum of six factors:

1. **Median household income.** Linear scale: $55,000/year earns zero points, $115,000/year earns the maximum 25. The idea is that income drives purchasing power, and purchasing power drives owner-occupier demand.
2. **Straight-line distance to CBD.** A stepped scale in 5km / 15km / 30km / 50km bands, capped at 20 points.
3. **Suburb type.** A lookup — inner-city 18, middle-ring 16, coastal 14, outer-metro 12, regional 8. Designed to reflect the long-run capital-growth base rate of the tier.
4. **Transport score.** Derived from amenity proximity (stations, bus routes, arterials). Up to 15 points.
5. **Amenity score.** OpenStreetMap POI density — schools, cafes, parks. Up to 10 points.
6. **Median weekly rent.** Up to 10 points, scaled against a state-by-state reference band.

The total is capped at 100. A suburb's band is one of four labels:

- **Strong** — 81 to 100 (strong fundamentals across the board)
- **Good** — 61 to 80 (most factors favourable)
- **Moderate** — 41 to 60 (mixed picture)
- **Weak** — 0 to 40 (structural headwinds)

Note that the score is descriptive, not predictive. It describes what the ABS 2021 numbers say about current conditions — it doesn't forecast returns. Past performance is not a guarantee of future performance, and nothing on our pages is financial advice.

## Why we don't score every suburb

Australia has 14,512 State Suburbs in the ABS SAL 2021 dataset. The vast majority are small rural localities with minimal market depth — scoring them would produce noise, not signal, and it would drag the overall quality of the site down in Google's eyes.

We use a four-factor gate to decide which suburbs get a full indexed profile:

- The suburb must have a valid Australia Post postcode.
- It must have at least 2,000 usual residents at the 2021 Census.
- It must have a median household income recorded in the ABS 2021 dataset.
- It must not be flagged `tiny` in our internal source data.

Against the current dataset, that leaves approximately **3,022 suburbs indexed** — roughly 21% of the SAL file. The other 11,490 suburbs remain reachable from the state hub "All localities" drawer but carry a `noindex, follow` robots tag, so Google does not rank them.

## Comparison tables — the uniqueness anchor

One thing we think hard about is making sure every suburb page is distinguishable from every other suburb page. A comparison table is a simple, powerful way to do that. For each indexed suburb we compute the state median across six fields (population, income, rent, mortgage, distance, dwelling mix), then show the delta as a percentage.

Two suburbs with different underlying numbers will always produce different tables — and different prose, because every sentence in the insight narrative is formula-driven off those same deltas.

## Rate sensitivity

The rate stress-test in the risk factors uses a rule-of-thumb approximation: a one-percentage-point RBA cash-rate rise on a 30-year mortgage costs approximately 10% more per month. That's a simplification — real repricing depends on the original loan rate, loan term, and fixed-vs-variable mix — but it's a directionally correct back-of-envelope for suburb comparison.

For a precise figure on your actual loan, use our [loan serviceability calculator](/tools/loan-serviceability-calculator/).

## Rental stress

We flag a suburb as having rental stress when the median weekly rent × 52 divided by median household income exceeds 30%. That's the long-standing Productivity Commission definition and it's the same threshold used by state housing authorities.

## Strategy verdicts

Each strategy card (Buy & Hold, Rental Yield, Renovation/Flip) is assigned a strength rating by a deterministic rule set:

- **Buy & Hold — strong** when income-vs-state is ≥ 1.15 AND (distance is ≤ 25km OR population is ≥ 10,000).
- **Rental Yield — strong** when the cash-flow coverage ratio is ≥ 85%.
- **Renovation — strong** when the house percentage is at least 10pp above the state median AND population is ≥ 5,000.

The exact thresholds are in `build/build-suburbs.js` in our public repository. Nothing is hand-tuned per suburb.

## What's coming next

Census 2026 data will be incorporated as soon as the ABS releases it (scheduled late 2026 / mid-2027). We'll version this post and the methodology page when that happens. Live sales and rental data (Domain / realestate.com.au) is on the roadmap but is not integrated today — when it is, we'll document the licensing and the refresh cadence on our [data sources page](/data-sources.html).

If you reproduce our numbers and land on a different answer, email [support@equitysight.app](mailto:support@equitysight.app) with your calculation. We respond within five business days and log every confirmed correction publicly.
author: James Patel
author_bio: Head of Property Data at EquitySight. Certified Practising Valuer (B.Prop, RMIT) with 12 years at two national valuation firms covering residential portfolios across VIC and NSW. Owns the ABS ingest, the scoring methodology, and the comparison-delta logic behind every suburb profile.
